extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners (patent attorneys/agents) and USPTO disciplinary staff
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, prohibited conduct, mitigating factors, and required remedial and probationary conditions governing disciplinary proceedings and settlement agreements for practitioners before the United States Patent and Trademark Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional basis for disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director has jurisdiction over practitioner discipline under 35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D) and 32, and the Office proceeds under 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.20(a) and 11.26.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceedings and settlement agreements must be brought and processed under these statutory and regulatory authorities; settlement submissions to the Under Secretary/Director must satisfy 37 C.F.R. § 11.26.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 10.23(b)(4) — Prohibition on dishonesty/fraud/deceit/misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 10.23(b)(4) proscribes engaging in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing checks drawn on an account without sufficient funds (resulting in returned checks) is cited as conduct violating this rule. Such conduct is considered dishonest conduct for disciplinary purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 10.23(b)(6) — Conduct reflecting adversely on fitness to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 10.23(b)(6) proscribes engaging in conduct that reflects adversely on a practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated financial or practice-management failures (e.g., multiple returned checks, delay in paying required fees) can be treated as reflecting adversely on fitness to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 10.112(b) — Prohibition on commingling client funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 10.112(b) proscribes commingling funds belonging to the practitioner or the practitioner's firm with advanced funds belonging to a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must deposit unearned client funds in a sequestered (IOLTA/escrow) account; advancing client fees from an operating account without maintaining escrow risks violation. The document finds failure to maintain an escrow account and commingling as a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 10.77(c) — Duty to avoid neglect of entrusted legal matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 10.77(c) proscribes neglect of an entrusted legal matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to timely pay USPTO fees for which a client advanced funds (leading to abandonment, late filings, or other client harm) is cited as neglect of an entrusted matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement agreement content requirements (37 C.F.R. § 11.26)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Proposed Settlement Agreement must set forth stipulated facts, legal conclusions, and sanctions and satisfy the requirements of 37 C.F.R. § 11.26.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order states that the Proposed Settlement Agreement resolves disciplinary action arising from stipulated facts and complies with § 11.26; practitioners and OED must include required elements when proposing settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Returned checks and USPTO fee-payment procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office treats returned checks as though the fee was never received; returned checks trigger requirements to pay the underlying fee, late surcharges, and returned-check processing fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notices such as 'Notice to File Missing Parts' and 'Notification Concerning Prescribed Fees' give one month or two months to cure; failure results in abandonment or invitation to pay with added late fees. Examples show returned-check fees ($50), late surcharges ($25 and larger for PCT), and invitation-to-pay late-payment penalties (e.g., hundreds of dollars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment and fee remediation expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners who issue dishonored checks are expected to pay the application fees, surcharges, and returned-check processing fees and any late-payment penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigating factor: Respondent paid the application fees and all outstanding returned-check processing fees required by 37 C.F.R. § 1.21(m). Timely remediation of outstanding fees is a relevant mitigating consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors relevant to discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that may mitigate discipline include (as articulated here) prompt payment of owing fees, payment of returned-check processing fees, absence of prior disciplinary history, undertaking remedial measures, and personal circumstances (e.g., serious prior injury).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order lists specific remedial steps (hiring accounting counsel, hiring bookkeepers, adopting new software, opening separate accounts) and the fact that no client reported substantial harm and no prior discipline as mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial practice-management measures demonstrating remediation
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopted remedial measures cited as evidence of remediation include: consulting outside counsel; retaining an accounting/bookkeeping firm; adopting Lexis-Nexis PCLaw billing and accounting; opening separate accounts (Operations, Petty Cash, PTO Fees, and an Escrow Account); using cashier's checks while policies developed; adopting a computerized tracking/calendar system; performing reconciliations of fees/payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These steps are presented as corrective actions that reduce the risk of recurrence and serve as mitigating evidence when assessing sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probationary structure and stayed suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: A suspension term may be stayed conditioned upon a probationary period with specified terms and conditions; if the practitioner satisfies probation terms the suspension may not be served.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Here, a 24-month suspension was stayed provided the respondent served and successfully completed a 24-month probation subject to enumerated conditions. The stay may be lifted for violations during probation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice-monitor requirement and reporting schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: During probation the practitioner must hire, at the practitioner's expense, a practice monitor acceptable to the OED Director to review the legal practice and prepare reports at six, 12, 18, and 24 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each report must indicate whether the practitioner is in compliance with specified USPTO professional-responsibility requirements; reports must identify implicated disciplinary rules and explain noncompliance if present. If a monitor cannot continue, the practitioner must promptly propose a replacement acceptable to OED.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring focus areas (IOLTA/escrow, trust & operating accounts, calendaring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice-monitor reports must state compliance regarding: (a) maintaining funds received from clients in IOLTA/escrow accounts, (b) managing law-practice trust and operating accounts, and (c) maintaining and using electronic and manual calendaring systems for timely rendering of services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The monitor should explicitly evaluate these discrete practice-management domains and identify any disciplinary rules implicated by noncompliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replacement of practice monitor and consequences for failure to maintain one
rubrics_metrics.description: If the practice monitor cannot continue, the practitioner must promptly provide OED the name, address, and resume of another proposed monitor for approval; failure to promptly name and maintain an acceptable monitor may be grounds for an Order to Show Cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deadlines for reports are not extended by failure to proffer a monitor except by written agreement; prolonged absence of an acceptable monitor can trigger enforcement steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement process for probation noncompliance (Order to Show Cause / lifting stay)
rubrics_metrics.description: If OED believes the practitioner failed to comply during probation, OED will issue an Order to Show Cause, give the practitioner 15 days to respond, and if OED remains of that view will forward the matter and evidence to the USPTO Director to seek lifting the stay and imposing suspension (up to the original suspension term).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets out procedural steps and timelines for enforcement and potential immediate suspension upon lifting the stay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and administrative effects of suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: If suspended, the practitioner must comply with 37 C.F.R. § 11.58; OED will disseminate information per 37 C.F.R. § 11.59; USPTO will dissociate the practitioner's name from customer numbers and PKI certificates; the practitioner may not use or obtain USPTO customer numbers or PKI certificates unless and until reinstated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspension triggers operational restrictions on USPTO systems access and public notice/discipline dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and notice obligations for discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: OED must publish the Final Order in the OED Reading Room and issue a Notice of Stayed Suspension in the Official Gazette; under 37 C.F.R. § 11.59 OED must notify state disciplinary authorities and courts in jurisdictions where the practitioner is admitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public dissemination is mandatory and includes specific publication outlets and cross-jurisdictional notices to enforcement agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client notice and affidavit requirement after discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.20(a)(4), the practitioner must provide a copy of the Final Order to affected clients within 30 days and file an affidavit with OED within 45 days certifying compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to timely notify clients and file the affidavit is a provable violation of the Final Order and may lead to further enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of record in future disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The record of the disciplinary proceeding, including the Final Order, will be considered in any future complaints or proceedings for the same or similar misconduct either as an aggravating factor or to rebut representations by or on behalf of the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior findings and settled facts can be used to increase discipline in future matters or to challenge later practitioner assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of costs in settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: The settlement provides that the OED Director and Respondent each bear their own costs incurred to date and in carrying out the agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlement agreements may include cost-allocation terms; parties should explicitly state who bears costs.
